title: Jump Game
description:
# Jump Game

You are given an integer array `nums`. You start at index `0`.

For each index `i`, `nums[i]` is the maximum number of steps you may jump forward from that index. You may choose any jump length from `1` through `nums[i]`, and you may not jump backward.

Return `true` if it is possible to reach the last index. Otherwise, return `false`.

## Example 1

**Input:** nums = [2,3,1,1,4]

**Output:** true

**Explanation:** Jump from index `0` to index `1`, then jump from index `1` to the last index.

## Example 2

**Input:** nums = [3,2,1,0,4]

**Output:** false

**Explanation:** Every reachable path gets stuck at or before index `3`; `nums[3]` is `0`, and the last index remains unreachable.

## Constraints

* `1 <= nums.length <= 10^4`
* `0 <= nums[i] <= 10^5`

solutions.name: Forward Greedy Farthest Reach
solutions.description:
## Approach

Scan from left to right while keeping `maxReach`, the farthest index reachable from positions already proven reachable. If the scan index ever becomes greater than `maxReach`, the path has fallen into an unreachable gap. If `maxReach` reaches the last index, the answer is true.

## Key Insight

Among all choices made before index `i`, only the farthest reachable boundary matters. The exact jump sequence can be ignored because any index at or before that boundary can be considered when its turn arrives.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Backward Greedy Goal Shrink
solutions.description:
## Approach

Start with the last index as the current `goal`. Scan from right to left. Whenever index `i` can jump to the current goal or beyond it, index `i` becomes the new goal. At the end, the start can reach the end exactly when the goal has moved to `0`.

## Key Insight

This reverses the question: instead of asking how far the start can reach, ask which earlier positions can already reach a known-good suffix. Each successful index expands that suffix leftward.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Forward Reachability DP Table
solutions.description:
## Approach

Create a boolean table where `reachable[i]` means index `i` can be reached from the start. For every reachable index, mark every index inside its jump range as reachable. After all relaxations, read the value for the last index.

## Key Insight

The array defines a directed acyclic reachability graph from smaller indices to larger indices. The DP table is the direct graph formulation that the greedy farthest-boundary solution later compresses.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Backward Good-Index DP
solutions.description:
## Approach

Mark the last index as good. Then scan indices from right to left. For each index, inspect the positions it can jump to; if any of them is already good, mark the current index as good. The answer is whether index `0` becomes good.

## Key Insight

A position is good exactly when it has an outgoing jump to another good position. This makes the recursive definition explicit without using recursion or risking stack depth on large inputs.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n^2)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Implicit BFS Frontier Expansion
solutions.description:
## Approach

Treat all indices reachable with the current number of jumps as one contiguous frontier ending at `currentEnd`. While scanning that frontier, compute the farthest index reachable by one more jump. If the frontier cannot expand, return false; if it reaches the last index, return true.

## Key Insight

Although the jump graph has many edges, the set of positions reachable after each jump count is a continuous interval. That lets us simulate BFS levels using only two boundary integers.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)
